title: Harvesting potatoes
subtitle: Lifting earlies to maincrops, curing for storage, and managing green tubers
excerpt: First early potatoes are lifted when the flowers open in June; maincrop potatoes are lifted in August and September when the haulm has died back. Maincrops need a two-week period after the haulm is cut before lifting to toughen the skins for storage.
sourceNotes: RHS potato growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on potato harvest and storage, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The top growth of a potato plant: stems, leaves, and any flowering structures. In late summer, the haulm yellows and dies back as the plant redirects its energy into the tubers. Cutting the haulm to 5 cm above the ground two weeks before lifting hardens the potato skins and reduces the spread of blight spores from foliage into the soil.

Potatoes exposed to light develop chlorophyll and solanine, a toxic alkaloid that causes the skin and flesh to turn green. Solanine is not destroyed by cooking. Green potatoes should not be eaten; cut away green areas generously if found. Greening is prevented by earthing up to keep all tubers covered, and by storing in complete darkness.

content.text: Potato harvest timing differs by type. First and second earlies are dug fresh when wanted, starting from June; they do not store well. Maincrop varieties are left to reach full maturity in August and September, with the
cut back first to toughen the skins.

Test from late June by scraping the skin of a tuber; if it rubs off easily, the potato is waxy and at its best. Dig as needed. Lift the plant fully with a fork; loosen the soil well away from the stems to avoid spearing tubers. First earlies do not keep long once lifted; plan to use within a week.

Wait for the haulm to yellow and die back naturally, usually August to September. Once the haulm is down, cut it to 5 cm and leave for two weeks before lifting; this hardens the skins and reduces blight spore transfer. Lift on a dry day. Leave tubers on the soil surface for a few hours to dry before storing.

Store only undamaged tubers with unbroken skins. In paper sacks or wooden boxes in the dark (never clear bags or plastic, which trap moisture and cause rot). A cool, frost-free shed or garage at 4 to 7°C is ideal. Check monthly; remove any going soft or rotten.
